newsitem.title: USA: Lieberman sees White House at centre of U.S. scandal.
newsitem.headline: Lieberman sees White House at centre of U.S. scandal.

text.p: By Alan Elsner, U.S. Political Correspondent

Senator Joseph Lieberman, a Democratic member of the committee investigating U.S. campaign fund-raising, says the Clinton administration was at the heart of a breakdown of the political finance system in 1996.

The Connecticut Democrat told Reuters in an interview this week he reached that conclusion after four weeks of hearings by the Senate Governmental Affairs Committee. The hearings are due to resume early next month.
"In 1996, the system of limits to campaign contributions and full disclosure collapsed. That was true of both parties," Lieberman said.
"In that sense, the Democratic administration was part of that breakdown, was at the centre of that breakdown," he said.

The committee, under the chairmanship of Tennessee's Republican Sen. Fred Thompson, is investigating the way foreign money, mainly from Asian business interests, illegally flowed into the U.S. political system in the 1996 campaign.

It is especially interested in discovering whether there was a systematical attempt by some Asian interests to buy favours or gain access to classified information or to influence U.S. foreign policy.

While most of the Democrats on the committee adopted the role of defence attorneys for their party and for the Clinton administration, Lieberman has emerged in a pivotal position because of his willingness to go after wrongdoings committed by fellow Democrats.
He said at the outset of the investigation he was determined to follow the money trail wherever it led and let the political chips fall where they may.

That approach has won Lieberman plaudits from some unlikely sources. Conservative columnist Arianna Huffington even suggested recently he might make a suitable vice presidential candidate in 2000, a possibility Lieberman dismissed with a laugh.
From what he has heard so far, Lieberman said he could not yet conclude there was an organised scheme to bring foreign money into the U.S. political system.
"We don't have enough evidence that there was a systematic plot to bring foreign money into the system but I have some suspicions based on the evidence," he said.
He said he was troubled by the failure of the White House and the Democratic National Committee to produce documents relevant to the investigation in a timely manner.
For example, the day after a hearing focused on the activities of Macao-based businessman Ng Lap Sing, the Clinton administration produced records that he had visited the White House 10 times.
That led to Thompson, with the unanimous backing of the committee, slapping a subpoena on the White House.
Then, last week, the DNC said it had unearthed thousands of pages of documents that had been subpoenaed in April, which it said had been discovered in a filing cabinet.

"These things raise our suspicions. I hear the denials. If it is an oversight, it's a troubling oversight. But I'm not encouraged by the cooperation we've been getting from the White House and the DNC," said Lieberman.
